# UNITED STATES v. SUMMERS (2026)
## United States Court of Appeals, Third Circuit.
### Counsel for Appellant, Alison Brill \[Argued\], Office of Federal Public Defender Counsel for Appellee, Mark E. Coyne, Steven G. Sanders \[Argued\], Office of United States Attorney
### UNITED STATES of America v. Charles SUMMERS, Appellant

### No. 25-2502

### Decided: October 06, 2026
### Counsel for Appellant, Alison Brill \[Argued\], Office of Federal Public Defender Counsel for Appellee, Mark E. Coyne, Steven G. Sanders \[Argued\], Office of United States Attorney
Defendant Charles Summers tried to rape a 13-year-old girl. He pleaded guilty in New York to that heinous crime. New York authorities warned him that he needed to register as a sex offender.
When he got out of jail in New York, he started to live and work in New Jersey. He did not register in his new state. That was a violation of the federal Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act, or SORNA.
Defendant pleaded guilty to his SORNA offense.

This is a two-issue sentencing appeal. First, Defendant argues that the District Court erred in its calculation of his Criminal History under the Guidelines. This part of the appeal is moot.
Defendant recently finished his jail sentence, and the District Court already sentenced him to the statutory minimum amount of supervised release. Thus, no effectual relief is available to him on this issue and we must dismiss this aspect of the appeal.
Second, Defendant challenges his classification as a Tier III SORNA offender, which is the most serious classification. See 34 U.S.C. § 20911.
Applying that approach here, we agree with the District Court that Defendant's New York sex crime qualifies for SORNA Tier III.

**USA v. Summers**

Charles Summers was convicted in New York of first-degree attempted rape of a 13-year-old girl.

Summers moved to New Jersey, where he failed to register as a sex offender, violating the Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act (SORNA). He was arrested in New Jersey for this federal offense, pleaded guilty, and was sentenced in the United States District Court for the District of New Jersey.

Summers appealed the Criminal History calculation and his Tier III SORNA classification to the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit.

While his appeal was pending, he completed his jail sentence and began serving supervised release.The United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit found that the Criminal History issue was moot because Summers had finished his prison term and was already serving the mandatory minimum supervised release, so no effectual relief could be granted on that point.

The Third Circuit adopted a hybrid categorical approach to compare the New York conviction with federal offenses and concluded that Summers's conviction matched the federal crime of attempted sexual abuse, justifying Tier III classification.

UNITED STATES of America v. Charles SUMMERS, Appellant
Opinion of the Court
Defendant Charles Summers tried to rape a 13-year-old girl. He pleaded guilty in New York to that heinous crime. New York authorities warned him that he needed to register as a sex offender. When he got out of jail in New York, he started to live and work in New Jersey. He did not register in his new state. That was a violation of the federal Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act, or SORNA. Defendant pleaded guilty to his SORNA offense.
This is a two-issue sentencing appeal. First, Defendant argues that the District Court erred in its calculation of his Criminal History under the Guidelines. This part of the appeal is moot. Defendant recently finished his jail sentence, and the District Court already sentenced him to the statutory minimum amount of supervised release. Thus, no effectual relief is available to him on this issue and we must dismiss this aspect of the appeal.
Second, Defendant challenges his classification as a Tier III SORNA offender, which is the most serious classification. See 34 U.S.C. § 20911. This issue is not moot because it impacts the duration of his registration requirement and the frequency of the related in-person reporting requirement.

United States v. Summers — Third Circuit affirms Tier III sex-offender classification

By  / October 6, 2026
Case United States of America v. Charles Summers Court U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit Judge Restrepo; Montgomery-Reeves; Bove Date Decided October 6, 2026 Docket No. 25-2502 Topics SORNA; sex-offender registration; sentencing; mootness Source Read the full opinion

Background

Charles Summers was convicted in New York in 2015 of first-degree attempted rape. After his release from prison, Summers began living and working in New Jersey in 2021 but did not notify New York of his address change or register as a sex offender in New Jersey.
Federal authorities arrested Summers in 2024 for violating the Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act (SORNA). He pleaded guilty. The District of New Jersey classified him as a Tier III SORNA offender, calculated a 24-to-30-month Guidelines range, and imposed 24 months’ imprisonment and the statutory minimum five years of supervised release. Summers completed his prison term while his appeal was pending.

The Court’s Holding

The Third Circuit dismissed as moot Summers’s challenge to the criminal-history calculation. Because he had finished his prison sentence and already received the mandatory minimum supervised-release term, a resentencing could not provide effectual relief. Possible benefits in separate state proceedings were too speculative to preserve a live controversy.
The court affirmed Summers’s Tier III classification. It adopted a hybrid categorical approach to SORNA tiering: courts compare the elements of the state offense with the listed federal offenses categorically, while determining victim age from records concerning the particular offense. Summers’s New York attempted-rape conviction categorically matched attempted sexual abuse under 18 U.S.C. § 2242(1), and the victim was 13 years old. The District Court sentenced Defendant in July 2025. The District Court determined that Defendant qualified as a Tier III sex offender, pursuant to U.S.S.G. § 2A3.5(a) and 34 U.S.C. § 20911 , based on his New York sex crime. The District Court then calculated a Guidelines range of 24 to 30 months based on Offense Level 13 and Criminal History Category IV. Following that calculation, the District Court imposed a sentence of 24 months’ imprisonment followed by 60 months’ supervised release.

Defendant timely appealed. He was released from prison while the appeal was pending. He is currently serving the term of supervised release.

The District Court had jurisdiction under 18 U.S.C. § 3231. We have jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1291 and 18 U.S.C. § 3742(a) . We review procedural-error sentencing claims for abuse of discretion, which includes de novo review of legal questions. *United States v. Jackson* , 132 F.4th 266, 272 (3d Cir. 2025) . 1

## II

Defendant challenges the District Court’s determinations regarding his Criminal History and placement in SORNA Tier III. The Criminal History issue is moot. The SORNA tiering issue is live, but we agree with the District Court’s conclusion.

The mootness doctrine prohibits courts from “pronounc[ing] on past actions that do not have any ‘continuing effect’ in the world.” *FBI v. Fikre* , 601 U.S. 234, 241 (2024) . The requirement is not satisfied, and a case is moot, “when it is impossible for a court to grant any effectual relief whatever to the prevailing party.” *Chafin v. Chafin* , 568 U.S. 165, 172 (2013) . To be effectual, “the relief sought must likely redress the purported injury.” *Mejia-Henriquez v. AG* , --- F.4th ----, 2026 WL 2489594, at *8 n.10 (3d Cir. 2026).

The District Court had jurisdiction under 18 U.S.C. § [3231](https://law.counselstack.com/usc/18/3231).
We have jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § [1291](https://law.counselstack.com/usc/28/1291) and 18 U.S.C. § [3742](https://law.counselstack.com/usc/18/3742)(a). We review procedural-error sentencing claims for abuse of discretion, which includes de novo review of legal questions. United States v. Jackson, [132 F.4th 266](https://law.counselstack.com/opinion/united-states-v-carolyn-jackson-ca3-2025), 272 (3d Cir. 2025).1 III.
Defendant challenges the District Court’s determinations regarding his Criminal History and placement in SORNA Tier III. The Criminal History issue is moot. The SORNA tiering issue is live, but we agree with the District Court’s conclusion.

The District Court was correct that Defendant is a Tier III offender under SORNA. We adopt the hybrid categorical approach employed by other Circuits to resolve the issue in this appeal. Under that approach, Defendant’s New York attempted-rape crime is a categorical match for attempted sexual abuse, in violation of 18 U.S.C. § [2242](https://law.counselstack.com/usc/18/2242)(1).

Based on the foregoing, we will dismiss the appeal insofar as Defendant challenges the District Court’s Criminal History calculation, otherwise affirm the judgment, and remand for the limited purpose of allowing the District Court to modify the judgment by memorializing that Defendant is a Tier III SORNA offender.

# UNITED STATES v. SUMMERS (2026)
## United States Court of Appeals, Third Circuit.
###
UNITED STATES of America v. Charles SUMMERS, Appellant
### No. 25-2502
### Decided: October 06, 2026
### Before: Restrepo, Montgomery-Reeves, and Bove, Circuit Judges

Opinion of the Court
Defendant Charles Summers tried to rape a 13-year-old girl. He pleaded guilty in New York to that heinous crime. New York authorities warned him that he needed to register as a sex offender. When he got out of jail in New York, he started to live and work in New Jersey. He did not register in his new state. That was a violation of the federal Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act, or SORNA. Defendant pleaded guilty to his SORNA offense.

The District Court had jurisdiction under 18 U.S.C. § 3231. We have jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1291 and 18 U.S.C. § 3742(a). We review procedural-error sentencing claims for abuse of discretion, which includes de novo review of legal questions. United States v. Jackson, 132 F.4th 266, 272 (3d Cir. 2025).1

Based on the foregoing, we will dismiss the appeal insofar as Defendant challenges the District Court's Criminal History calculation, otherwise affirm the judgment, and remand for the limited purpose of allowing the District Court to modify the judgment by memorializing that Defendant is a Tier III SORNA offender.
